newsitem.title: UK: 50 more years of IRA bombs won't budge us - Major.
newsitem.headline: 50 more years of IRA bombs won't budge us - Major.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major insisted on Wednesday that Britain would not give way to violence even if the Irish Republican Army continued its bombing campaign for another 50 years.

Major said he was confident that a deadlock in the Northern Irish peace process could be ended but insisted that Britain would not be swayed by bombs into allowing the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing to join in peace talks.
"If the IRA continues with violence for the next 50 years then Britain would not change its policy in the face of that violence for the next 50 years," Major said.
"The British government's position would be unmovable," he told the Belfast Telegraph newspaper.
"You cannot bomb Britain out of a political position and you cannot bomb your way into the objectives that Sinn Fein seek."

Major, making a traditional Christmas visit to troops and community leaders in British province, said he was totally committed to the three-year drive to end a decades-old conflict in which thousands of Protestants and Catholics have died.

"We have now hit a hurdle but I think it is a hurdle we will be able to overcome. We have done so in the past. I have every intention of trying to do so again," he told reporters after visiting a school in the town of Dungannon near Belfast.
"I don't believe people can stand in the way of that progress. It may be slow, it may be painful but progress I am confident there will be," he said.
Major's optimism is not shared by many local politicians and security analysts, who are gloomy about the short-term prospects for peace in the war-weary region.

The IRA shows no sign of restoring a ceasefire it abandoned last February and multi-party talks that have limped along since June are due to adjourn for Christmas next week with politicians saying there is no sign of a breakthrough.

"I hope from where we are that we will be able to move forwards," said Major, on his first visit to Northern Ireland since Irish Republican Army bombers struck at the heart of Britain's military presence here in October.
Britain is adamant that the IRA must declare a truce before Sinn Fein is allowed into the talks, while Sinn Fein wants talks without preconditions.
Irish nationalist hopes for a new truce received a setback recently when Major rejected proposals from Catholic moderate leader John Hume aimed at speeding Sinn Fein's access to talks.
Meanwhile, tension is building up. IRA guerrillas fighting British rule killed a soldier in a car bomb attack at British military headquarters in Lisburn on October 7.
It was the first IRA attack in Northern Ireland for two years and came nine months after the guerrillas went back to a war footing with bombs on mainland Britain.
Recent explosives and armaments finds have fuelled British fears that republican guerrillas are planning further attacks.

Northern Ireland's 60 per cent Protestant majority strongly supports rule from London, but the Catholic minority, some of whom back the IRA and its Sinn Fein political arm, want an all-Ireland state ruled from Dublin.
